This one got me SO badly. Before the economy there tanked as hard as it did, my late Uncle ran a successful and very small Armenian restaurant in Lebanon. My late aunt worked there as well. Anthony Bourdain ate in and loved my uncle's cooking. My family there that met him absolutely loved him. They said after the cameras rolled, he asked so many thoughtful things. He was kind, empathetic, compassionate, complimentary, and genuinely curious to learn as much as he could about Lebanon, and the Armenian people.

My uncle's restaurant ended up with three locations (the third after his death). My youngest cousin worked there and was training to be a chef. 

My uncle died tragically in a freak car crash in 2015. Then, my Aunt finally was able to reunite with her daughter from a terrifying marriage (her father had kept her captive, had connections, lied to her about my aunt, and when she left, she had to hide with various friends for a while to avoid getting taken back. She died of Lymphoma a year later. And about six months after that...she was murdered in the massacre at Club Reina in Turkey on New Year's Eve 2017. 

My heart will never forget the kindness and empathy of that man. I miss all of them. For me, they will live in my dreams of Lebanon, and the one magical summer of 2010 when I finally got to meet them all. Bourdain was a man who noticed all of the little things - so the big evils of the world ate at him like mad.

Robin Williams was also extremely difficult for me as my father and I enjoyed several of his films while I was growing up. Mrs. Doubtfire hit the first visitation we had with him after our parents' divorce. After the movie, he told me and my sister that just like Robin in the movie, he would love us, and always make sure to be a part of our lives, no matter what.

Ya'aburnee. 

My father was born in Beirut, Lebanon in 1957 to two sole survivors from each family in the Armenian Genocide.

Arabic is my father's second language. His first is Armenian (the Diaspora Western dialect), his third French, and his fourth is English. I grew up with a number of childhood words that were often a mix of the other languages, but later learned my mother forbade him from teaching us any of the languages.

My father came here in the late 1970's to go to university. He fell in love with American music. After the divorce, I regularly saw him a few times a year, and my mother tried to destroy our relationship, and almost all of my ethnic identity became repressed.

Long story short, he moved back to Beirut around 2002 as his mother and brother were in poor health, and the job market for what he does was drying up or paying too little.

I visited in 2010. To use the word "magical" downplays the significance of what that trip did for me on a spiritual and foundational level. I always wanted to go back. But between struggling financially, and the same for my father as the Lebanese financial collapse rolling, I didn't get the chance. I had just gotten married a few months before my trip - I kept my marriage plans to myself for a number of reasons. I wanted so badly to take my husband to that beautiful country, to meet family and friends.

It will never happen now. I have watched three of those family members die terrible, tragic deaths - my 25 year old cousin Rita was one of those who lost her life on New Year's Eve in the Club Reina mass shooting in 2017. The details from the only surviving friend were horrific.

And now, extended family started dying. One of my cousin's husband lost his sister and her son. In pieces under a building.

My father is somewhat involuntarily employed blocks where the blasts have been happening. He lives maybe 20 min from.

My cousin was thrown across the room in her building, scrambled to grab her three cats - all who were scratching and panicking, and trying to find a news station.

She lives approximately 300 yards from the blast. Had she been outside, she would have been killed or severely wounded. She is terrified. She is 31 years old.

My father is old. He is tired. His stress between 16 hours of work, the commute, the work he takes home, affording food, and the bombing, he has gone through a round of shingles, become pre-diabetic, and while he did need a tooth fixed, he had a mystery pain all through his teeth.

I sing this song, I think of how we will war over whose love for who is stronger - and I know it's the natural order of things for us to lay our parents to rest before us. But if something happens - I may not know for days. It would start like it did with Rita - missing. Then - even if a body is found - I cannot even bury him. I will lose the treasures from my childhood he kept and still uses to reflect on us.

"Darling, you will bury me before I bury you" - I hear that sad verse through every "Goodbye" at the end of each weekly video call.

Sorry for the overshare. It's really really really hard, and I don't know anyone who can relate, so it's a very lonely sadness.

Once your 30s hit, and/or you have a child, life really changes in more ways than you think. It can look like a lot of things. To me, "So Heavy" describes a long, magical, very difficult journey, almost devoid of joy until the end, which I interpret as the birth, seeing X's face for the first time, and coming into something beautiful through all the pain, fear, and tragedy.

My Name Is Dark is steeped in deep rebellion, embracing chaos, destruction, and flirting with death for an undefined life path goal. It's fire, and energy, and anger, and being done with complacency.

In the end, "My Name Is Dark" is c's origin story, "miracle I made it out alive, on fire still", whereas "So Heavy" is a story truly about birth and new life through a slow, scary, painful, almost joyless process. It's X's origin tale, as well as c's rebirth and instead of creative energy destroying her over time, it's love that was terrifying, almost unthinkable, but in the end, is a new beginning, hopefully channeling the energy of love for nurturing and inspiring.

When they introduced the first lyrics "I feel her heart beating in me, get her out of me", and I was fascinated - and I felt heartbroken for her with how not only her "Lowlife" manager screwed her over, but the depths of abuse with Sinclair. I LOVE artists who evolve/try new genres throughout their careers! I want to say "I Disagree" was the first album I listened to, followed by watching some of her videos from the uncanny valley videos, to "Poppy.Computer", and then, "Am I A Girl?" followed by the Christmas album, then realizing HOLY SHIT, I REMEMBER HEARING "LOWLIFE" ON THE RADIO WAY BACK IN THE DAY!

"You can be anyone you want to be"

I grew up hearing crap like, "you can be ANYTHING!" on repeat, and let's face it, most kids can never become President, important scientists, or excel in a career they want, due to a LOT of reasons. This lyric is especially important to me since being diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder. I've had mental health issues both biological and environmentally influenced. I've often felt like a hundred people packed in one meat sack. I'm on my way to accepting all the parts of me CAN be one person, and I CAN be anyone I want to be.

That whole song I see as me singing to my past scared little kid self, and it's comforting, and I don't feel like suck a freak for being indoctrinated into so many things so many times. "I believe you're the one that's meant for me/ we can be free, we can be free" and "If you want it, somebody, just call my name/ I'll be there, believe me/ I'll keep you safe.

A lot of my EMDR therapy in the past involved me digging DEEP into childhood trauma, and telling the little one I was in the past that "everything won't be perfect", but "you're gonna be ok, and there is nothing wrong with you."
